lia3.title: Balancing Test
lia3.description: Balance interests against data subject rights

lia4.title: Safeguards
lia4.description: Document safeguards to protect data subjects

liav2_s1.title: Purpose Test
liav2_s1.description: Identify the legitimate interest being pursued.

liav2_s2.title: Necessity Test
liav2_s2.description: Assess whether the processing is necessary for that interest.

liav2_s3.title: Balancing Test
liav2_s3.description: Weigh the interest against the individual's rights and freedoms.

liav2_s4.title: Safeguards and outcome
liav2_s4.description: Record the safeguards that protect data subjects and the conclusion.

lia1_1.text: What is the legitimate interest being pursued?
lia1_1.helpText: Describe the specific interest, not just 'business purposes'

lia1_2.text: Is this interest recognized as legitimate under law?

lia1_3.text: What benefit does pursuing this interest provide?

lia2_1.text: Is the processing necessary to achieve the interest?

lia2_2.text: Are there less intrusive ways to achieve the same goal?

lia3_1.text: What is the nature of the data being processed?

lia3_2.text: Would data subjects reasonably expect this processing?

lia3_3.text: What is the potential impact on data subjects?

lia4_1.text: What safeguards are in place to protect data subjects?

lia4_2.text: Have you provided clear privacy information about this processing?

liav2_1_1.text: Whose legitimate interest is being pursued?
liav2_1_1.helpText: The interest may be the controller's or a third party's. Say whose it is, because the balancing test weighs it against the individual's rights. Example: "Our own interest in preventing fraud." Source: GDPR Art. 6(1)(f).
options: Both ours and a third party's

liav2_1_2.helpText: Name a specific interest, not just "business purposes". A clearly articulated, real and present interest is the first thing the test requires. Example: "Detecting fraudulent transactions to protect customers and the business." Source: GDPR Art. 6(1)(f) and Recital 47.

liav2_1_3.text: Is the interest lawful, clearly articulated and real (not speculative)?
liav2_1_3.helpText: An interest can only be relied on if it is lawful, precise enough to weigh, and a real interest rather than a hypothetical one. Example: "Yes: fraud prevention is lawful, specific and ongoing." Source: GDPR Art. 6(1)(f); EDPB guidance on legitimate interest.

liav2_2_1.text: Is the processing necessary to achieve the interest?
liav2_2_1.helpText: "Necessary" means the processing is a targeted and proportionate way to meet the interest, not merely useful. If it is only convenient, legitimate interest is not the right basis. Example: "Reasonably necessary: fraud scoring needs the transaction data." Source: GDPR Art. 6(1)(f).

liav2_2_2.text: Could a less intrusive means achieve the same result?
liav2_2_2.helpText: If a less intrusive way exists that is reasonably effective, you should use it instead. Example: "No: aggregated data would miss the individual fraud patterns." Source: GDPR Art. 6(1)(f); principle of data minimization, Art. 5(1)(c).
options: No, this is the least intrusive means
A less intrusive means exists but is far less effective
A less intrusive means is available

liav2_2_3.text: Is the data limited to what the interest requires (data minimization)?
liav2_2_3.helpText: Only the data genuinely needed for the interest should be processed. Example: "Yes: we use the transaction and device data, not the full customer profile." Source: GDPR Art. 5(1)(c).

liav2_3_1.text: What is the nature of the data?
liav2_3_1.helpText: The more sensitive the data, the heavier it weighs against the interest. Special category and criminal-offense data need a separate condition and rarely sit under legitimate interest alone. Example: "No special category data." Source: GDPR Arts. 9 and 10.
options: No special category or criminal-offense data
Includes special category or criminal-offense data

liav2_3_2.text: Would data subjects reasonably expect this processing?
liav2_3_2.helpText: Reasonable expectations turn on the relationship and how the data was collected. The less expected, the harder the interest is to justify. Example: "Clearly expected: customers expect fraud checks on payments." Source: GDPR Recital 47.

liav2_3_3.text: What is the likely impact on the individual?
liav2_3_3.helpText: Consider the effect on the person, including any decision made about them. A significant negative impact usually tips the balance towards their rights. Example: "Minor: a flagged payment may be delayed briefly." Source: GDPR Art. 6(1)(f).

liav2_3_4.text: Are children or other vulnerable people affected?
liav2_3_4.helpText: Children and vulnerable people warrant extra weight on their side of the balance. Example: "No: the service is for account holders aged 18 and over." Source: GDPR Recital 38; Art. 6(1)(f).

liav2_3_5.helpText: State the conclusion of the balance, taking the safeguards below into account. Where rights prevail, choose another lawful basis. Example: "Balanced; the right to object and data minimization are decisive." Source: GDPR Art. 6(1)(f).
options: The individual's rights prevail (do not rely on legitimate interest)

liav2_4_1.helpText: Safeguards can tip a finely balanced case in favor of the interest. List the ones actually in place. Example: "Right to object honored, retention limits, pseudonymization." Source: GDPR Arts. 21 and 5(1); Recital 47.
options: The right to object is honored

liav2_4_2.text: Have you told individuals about this processing and their right to object?
liav2_4_2.helpText: Individuals must be told, in the privacy notice, that you rely on legitimate interest and that they can object. Example: "Yes: the privacy notice names the interest and explains how to object." Source: GDPR Arts. 13(1)(d), 14(2)(b) and 21.

liav2_4_3.helpText: Summarize the outcome and any conditions that must hold for the processing to remain justified. Example: "May proceed while the right to object is honored and retention stays at 12 months." Source: GDPR Art. 6(1)(f).

customv2_1_1.text: What is the purpose of this assessment?
customv2_1_1.helpText: Say what you are evaluating and why, so the reader knows the scope. Example: "Reviewing a new marketing analytics tool before launch." Source: GDPR Art. 24 (accountability).

customv2_1_2.text: What is the scope of this assessment?
customv2_1_2.helpText: Define the systems, processes or data flows in scope, and anything left out. Example: "The web analytics pipeline; excludes the CRM." Source: GDPR Art. 24.

customv2_2_1.text: What are the key risks identified?
customv2_2_1.helpText: Name the concrete risks to individuals or to compliance, not generic ones. Example: "Tracking without consent; over-collection of behavioral data." Source: GDPR Art. 24.

customv2_2_2.text: What is the overall risk level?
customv2_2_2.helpText: Give a single overall rating for the risks above, before mitigation. Example: "Medium." Source: GDPR Art. 24.

customv2_3_1.text: What mitigations are in place or recommended?
customv2_3_1.helpText: List the measures that reduce the risks and who owns them. Example: "Consent banner before any tracking; retention capped at 14 months." Source: GDPR Art. 24.

customv2_3_2.helpText: State whether the risk that remains after mitigation is acceptable, and under what conditions. Example: "Acceptable with conditions: launch after the consent banner is live." Source: GDPR Art. 24.

tia1.title: Transfer Description
tia1.description: Describe the data transfer, including the parties involved, the data categories, and the transfer mechanism

tia2.title: Destination Country Legal Framework
tia2.description: Assess whether the laws and practices of the destination country provide an essentially equivalent level of protection to the EU/EEA

tia3.title: Supplementary Measures
tia3.description: Identify technical, contractual, and organizational measures that supplement the transfer mechanism to ensure an equivalent level of protection

tia4.title: Risk Assessment & Conclusion
tia4.description: Weigh the residual risk after supplementary measures and determine whether the transfer can proceed

tia5.title: Ongoing Monitoring
tia5.description: Define how the transfer will be monitored and when this assessment should be reviewed

tiav2_s1.title: The transfer
tiav2_s1.description: Describe the transfer, its tool, the data and the parties.

tiav2_s2.title: Destination laws and practices
tiav2_s2.description: Assess whether the destination gives essentially equivalent protection.

tiav2_s3.title: Supplementary Measures
tiav2_s3.description: Identify measures that supplement the transfer tool.

tiav2_s4.title: Risk and conclusion
tiav2_s4.description: Weigh the residual risk and decide whether the transfer can proceed.

tiav2_s5.title: Re-evaluation
tiav2_s5.description: Define how the transfer is monitored and when it is reviewed.

tia1_1.text: What personal data is being transferred?
tia1_1.helpText: Describe the categories of personal data (e.g., contact details, behavioral data, special categories) and estimated volume

tia1_2.text: Who is the data exporter and who is the data importer?
tia1_2.helpText: Name the organizations, their roles (controller/processor), and the countries they are established in

tia1_3.text: What is the transfer mechanism (Article 46 GDPR)?

tia1_4.text: What is the purpose of the transfer?

tia1_5.text: Is the transfer onward-transferred to a further third country?

tia2_1.text: Does the destination country have an EU adequacy decision?

tia2_2.text: Does the destination country have legislation permitting government access to personal data (e.g., surveillance, national security)?
options: Legislation exists but with effective oversight and safeguards
Broad surveillance powers with limited oversight
Mass surveillance or no independent judicial oversight

tia2_3.text: Describe the relevant laws and government access practices in the destination country
tia2_3.helpText: Reference specific legislation (e.g., FISA Section 702, UK IPA 2016, CLOUD Act). Include publicly available government access reports and transparency data where possible.

tia2_4.text: Is the data importer subject to government access requests in practice?
options: No: data importer has never received a government access request
Possible: data importer operates in a sector that may be targeted
Yes: data importer publishes transparency reports confirming access requests

tia2_5.text: Are effective legal remedies available to EU data subjects in the destination country?
options: Partial: administrative remedies but no judicial review

tia3_1.text: What technical measures are in place?
tia3_1.helpText: Select all technical measures that apply. Effective encryption with EU-held keys is the strongest technical safeguard.
options: Encryption at rest (importer cannot access keys)
Split processing (no single party sees full dataset)

tia3_2.text: What contractual measures supplement the SCCs or transfer agreement?
options: Obligation to challenge government access requests
Obligation to notify exporter of government access (where legally permitted)
Prohibition on onward transfers without prior authorization
Audit rights for the data exporter
Data localisation obligation (processing only in specified countries)
Suspension / termination clause if legal framework changes

tia3_3.text: What organizational measures are in place?
options: Internal policies restricting government access response procedures
Staff training on data protection obligations
Designated privacy / compliance team at the importer
Regular compliance audits or certifications (e.g., ISO 27001, SOC 2)
Incident response plan covering government access scenarios

tia3_4.text: Are the supplementary measures effective at preventing or mitigating the identified risks?
tia3_4.helpText: Explain why the combination of measures above is sufficient (or insufficient) to ensure essentially equivalent protection. If the data must be available in the clear to the importer (e.g., for processing), encryption alone may not be effective against government access orders.

tia4_1.text: What is the likelihood that public authorities in the destination country will access the transferred data?
options: Negligible: sector/data type not targeted, strong safeguards
Low: possible but unlikely given safeguards and data type
Medium: sector is known to be targeted; safeguards may not fully prevent access
High: evidence of routine access to this type of data/sector

tia4_2.text: What would be the severity of impact on data subjects if their data were accessed?
options: Negligible: pseudonymized or non-sensitive data, minimal harm
Low: limited personal data, low sensitivity
Medium: identifiable personal data, moderate sensitivity
High: special category data, vulnerable individuals, or potential for significant harm

tia4_3.text: Overall conclusion: can the transfer proceed?
options: Yes: supplementary measures provide essentially equivalent protection
Yes, with conditions: additional measures required before transfer can proceed
No: residual risk is too high; transfer should be suspended or alternative mechanism sought

tia4_4.text: If additional conditions are required, describe them
tia4_4.helpText: List specific actions that must be completed before the transfer can proceed (e.g., implement EU-held encryption keys, switch to a different processor).

tia5_1.text: How will changes in the destination country's legal framework be monitored?
tia5_1.helpText: Describe how you will track legislative changes, court rulings, and enforcement actions (e.g., subscribe to EDPB/SA updates, legal counsel monitoring, vendor transparency reports).

tia5_2.text: What events should trigger a reassessment?
options: New legislation or executive order in the destination country
Data importer receives a government access request
Change in data categories or volume transferred
Change of sub-processor or onward transfer
Supervisory authority guidance or enforcement action

tia5_3.text: When is the next scheduled review?
tia5_3.helpText: Provide a specific date or timeframe (e.g., 'within 12 months' or '2027-04-01').

tiav2_1_1.text: Which transfer tool are you relying on?
tiav2_1_1.helpText: The transfer tool is the legal basis for sending the data abroad. Where an adequacy decision covers the destination, no supplementary measures are needed. Example: "Standard Contractual Clauses." Source: GDPR Arts. 45 to 49.

tiav2_1_2.helpText: The 2021 Standard Contractual Clauses have four modules for the roles of the exporter and importer. Pick the one that matches. Example: "Module 2: we are the controller, the importer is our processor." Source: Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914.

tiav2_1_3.text: What categories of personal data are transferred?
tiav2_1_3.helpText: The sensitivity and volume of the data drive the risk of the transfer. Name every category, because special category and criminal-offense data raise the bar. Example: "Contact details, identifiers, behavioral data." Source: EDPB Recommendations 01/2020, step 1.

tiav2_1_4.text: Who is the exporter and who is the importer, and in which countries?
tiav2_1_4.helpText: Name the organizations, their roles (controller or processor) and the countries of establishment, so the transfer is fully mapped. Example: "We (controller, Spain) to our hosting provider (processor, United States)." Source: EDPB Recommendations 01/2020, step 1.

tiav2_1_5.text: Is the data onward-transferred to a further third country?
tiav2_1_5.helpText: An onward transfer to a further country extends the chain of risk and must itself be covered. Example: "Yes: the importer uses a sub-processor in a third country." Source: EDPB Recommendations 01/2020.

tiav2_2_1.text: Does the destination country have an EU adequacy decision?
tiav2_2_1.helpText: Adequacy means the Commission has found the country's protection essentially equivalent. Without it, you must assess the laws and practices yourself. Example: "No adequacy decision." Source: GDPR Art. 45.

tiav2_2_2.text: Does the destination's law allow disproportionate government access to data?
tiav2_2_2.helpText: The core Schrems II question: can public authorities reach the data in ways that would not be acceptable in the EU? Name the laws. Example: "Broad surveillance powers: FISA Section 702 and EO 12333." Source: EDPB Recommendations 01/2020, step 3.
options: Access exists but with effective oversight and safeguards
Broad surveillance powers with limited oversight
Mass surveillance or no independent judicial oversight

tiav2_2_3.text: Is the importer subject to government access requests in practice?
tiav2_2_3.helpText: Law on the books matters less if it is not applied to this importer; but a real risk in the sector counts against the transfer. Example: "Possible: cloud providers are within scope of the access law." Source: EDPB Recommendations 01/2020, step 3.
options: No: never received such a request
Possible: operates in a sector that may be targeted

tiav2_2_4.text: Are effective legal remedies available to EU data subjects there?
tiav2_2_4.helpText: Essentially equivalent protection includes a real way for individuals to challenge access to their data. Example: "Partial: an ombudsperson mechanism but no court review." Source: EDPB Recommendations 01/2020, step 3; GDPR Art. 47 of the Charter.

tiav2_2_5.text: Describe the relevant laws and government access practices.
tiav2_2_5.helpText: Cite specific legislation and any public government-access or transparency reports. Example: "FISA Section 702 permits access to data held by electronic communication service providers; the importer's transparency report shows N requests." Source: EDPB Recommendations 01/2020, step 3.

tiav2_3_1.text: Which technical measures are in place?
tiav2_3_1.helpText: Effective encryption with keys held outside the destination is the strongest technical safeguard against government access. Example: "Encryption at rest with EU-held keys and pseudonymization." Source: EDPB Recommendations 01/2020, Annex 2.
options: Encryption at rest, importer cannot access the keys

tiav2_3_2.text: Which contractual measures supplement the transfer tool?
tiav2_3_2.helpText: Contract terms bind the importer to resist and report access and to let the exporter act. Example: "Duty to challenge and to notify, plus a suspension clause." Source: EDPB Recommendations 01/2020, Annex 2; SCC clause 15.
options: Duty to challenge government access requests
Duty to notify the exporter of access (where lawful)
No onward transfer without prior authorization
Suspension or termination if the law changes

tiav2_3_3.text: Which organizational measures are in place?
tiav2_3_3.helpText: Organizational measures back up the technical and contractual ones with people and procedures. Example: "A documented access-request policy and annual ISO 27001 certification." Source: EDPB Recommendations 01/2020, Annex 2.
options: Internal policy for responding to access requests
A designated privacy or compliance team at the importer
Incident response plan covering access scenarios

tiav2_3_4.text: Are the measures effective against the identified risks? Explain.
tiav2_3_4.helpText: Explain why the measures together do, or do not, bring the protection up to an essentially equivalent level. If the importer must access the data in the clear, encryption may not help against an access order. Example: "Effective: data is pseudonymized and keys stay in the EU." Source: EDPB Recommendations 01/2020, step 4.

tiav2_4_1.text: How likely is government access to the transferred data?
tiav2_4_1.helpText: Combine the destination's laws and practices with the data type and the safeguards. Example: "Low: pseudonymized data, keys in the EU, sector not routinely targeted." Source: EDPB Recommendations 01/2020, step 3.

tiav2_4_2.text: How severe would the impact on data subjects be if accessed?
tiav2_4_2.helpText: Weigh the harm to individuals if their data were accessed, given its sensitivity. Example: "Medium: identifiable contact and usage data." Source: EDPB Recommendations 01/2020, step 3.

tiav2_4_3.helpText: The overall conclusion of the assessment. Where the risk cannot be brought down, the transfer should not proceed on this tool. Example: "Yes, with conditions: implement EU-held keys first." Source: EDPB Recommendations 01/2020, step 6.
options: No: residual risk too high, suspend or find another route

tiav2_4_4.text: If conditions are required, describe them.
tiav2_4_4.helpText: List the specific actions that must be completed before or during the transfer. Example: "Move key management to the EU; add a suspension clause to the contract." Source: EDPB Recommendations 01/2020, step 6.

tiav2_5_1.text: Which events should trigger a re-assessment?
tiav2_5_1.helpText: A transfer assessment is not one-off: name the events that reopen it. Example: "New access legislation; any access request; a 12-month review." Source: EDPB Recommendations 01/2020, step 6.
options: New legislation or executive order in the destination
The importer receives a government access request
Change in data categories or volume
Change of sub-processor or onward transfer

tiav2_5_2.text: When is the next scheduled review?
tiav2_5_2.helpText: Give a specific date, in the form YYYY-MM-DD. Example: "2027-04-01." Source: EDPB Recommendations 01/2020, step 6.

q0_1.text: Which frameworks does this assessment have to satisfy?
q0_1.helpText: Select one or both. The report lists every requirement of the frameworks selected and marks each one covered or outstanding. Sources: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Articles 35 and 36; California Code of Regulations, title 11, division 6, chapter 1, article 10.
options: California: CCPA risk assessment regulations, 11 CCR article 10

q8_1.text: Which California risk assessment triggers does the processing meet?
q8_1.helpText: Any one of them means a risk assessment is required. If none apply, the report says so plainly and claims no Californian requirement. Source: 11 CCR 7150(b).
options: Automated decision-making technology (ADMT) for a significant decision
Automated observation of employees, contractors, job applicants or students
Inferring sensitive traits from presence at a sensitive location
Processing to train ADMT, biometric or profiling technology

q8_2.helpText: How the personal information is collected, from which sources, how long it is kept, how many consumers it concerns, who it is disclosed to, and the technology used. Source: 11 CCR 7152(a)(3).

q8_3.text: Benefits of the processing to the business, the consumer, other stakeholders and the public

q8_4.helpText: Describe each impact, who it falls on and how serious it is. Source: 11 CCR 7152(a)(5).

q8_5.text: Safeguards planned to address the negative impacts

q8_6.text: Will the business start or continue the processing?
q8_6.helpText: Weigh the negative impacts, as mitigated by the safeguards, against the benefits. Source: 11 CCR 7152(a)(7).
options: Yes: the benefits outweigh the negative impacts once the safeguards are in place
No: the negative impacts outweigh the benefits

q8_7.text: Names and positions of the people who prepared, reviewed and approved this assessment

q8_8.text: Dates on which this assessment was reviewed and approved

q9_1.text: When is this assessment being conducted, in relation to the processing?
options: The processing is already under way

q9_2.text: Review and update schedule, the change that brings a review forward, and how long this assessment is kept

q9_3.text: Submission to the California Privacy Protection Agency by 1 April 2028
options: Not applicable: no trigger is met

q9_4.text: Executive who will attest to this assessment (name and position)

q9_5.text: Can the full assessment be provided within 30 days of a request from the agency or the Attorney General?

q1_7.helpText: Name the interest, whose interest it is (yours or a third party's) and why the processing is needed for it. Source: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Article 35(7)(a).

q4_3.text: The views of data subjects or their representatives, or the reason for not seeking them
q4_3.helpText: Record what was asked, who answered and what came of it. Where seeking those views is not appropriate, record why. Source: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Article 35(9).

q7_5.text: Prior consultation with the supervisory authority: date of the request, and the outcome or its status
q7_5.helpText: The processing may not start until the authority has answered or the period of Article 36(2) has passed. Record the date the consultation was sent, the authority, and its written advice once received. Source: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Article 36(1) and (2).

q7_4.text: When this assessment will be reviewed, and the change in risk that brings the review forward
q7_4.helpText: Give a review date and name the changes that require an earlier review, such as a new purpose, a new recipient or a new technology. Source: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Article 35(11).

hd1_1.text: Which jurisdictions apply to this processing?
hd1_1.helpText: Select every jurisdiction whose residents' data is collected or used. Changing the selection changes the questions below and the report. Source: DPO Central jurisdiction catalogue (GDPR, UK GDPR, CCPA/CPRA, MODPA, CTDPA, CPA, VCDPA, TDPSA, OCPA); Washington and Nevada are not in the catalogue.
options: Another US state with a comprehensive privacy law

hd1_2.text: Which CCPA risk-assessment triggers does the processing meet?
hd1_2.helpText: Any trigger means a risk assessment is required. Source: 11 CCR 7150(b) (checked 16 September 2026).
options: Automated decision-making technology (ADMT) for a significant decision
Automated observation of employees, contractors, job applicants or students
Inferring sensitive traits from presence at a sensitive location
Processing to train ADMT, biometric or profiling technology

hd1_3.helpText: Any case means a DPIA is required before the processing starts. Source: GDPR Art. 35(3)(a) to (c), as used in the DPO Central risk mappings and DPIA template.
options: Systematic and extensive evaluation, including profiling, with legal or similarly significant effects (Art. 35(3)(a))
Large-scale processing of special category data, such as health data (Art. 35(3)(b))
Systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area on a large scale (Art. 35(3)(c))
None of these, but the processing is still likely to be high risk

hd1_4.text: Which US state data protection assessment triggers apply?
hd1_4.helpText: Any trigger means a data protection assessment is required in the states selected. Source: DPO Central jurisdiction catalogue, VCDPA and CTDPA entry. The trigger list varies by state [to verify for each state].
options: Profiling with a foreseeable risk of harm
No assessment is required (reasons recorded in the notes)

hd2_1.text: What is the specific business purpose of the processing?
hd2_1.helpText: Name the campaign, measurement or audience use; avoid general wording such as "marketing". Source: 11 CCR 7152(a)(1) to (3); GDPR Art. 35(7)(a) (checked 16 September 2026).

hd2_2.text: Why is each category of data necessary for that purpose, and what less intrusive alternatives did you consider?

hd2_3.text: Which data minimisation measures apply (fields excluded, parameters removed, aggregation)?
hd2_3.helpText: Maryland limits collection to what is reasonably necessary. Source: DPO Central jurisdiction catalogue, MODPA entry.

hd2_4.text: Which GDPR legal basis and, for health data, which Article 9(2) condition do you rely on?
hd2_4.helpText: An Article 9(2) condition must be identified for each special category. For health data used in advertising, explicit consent is usually the only available condition [to verify]. Legitimate interest can only support data that is not special category data. Source: DPO Central DPIA auto-fill rules (Art. 9(2)) and DPIA template (Art. 6 bases).
options: Legitimate interests (Art. 6(1)(f)), with no special category data

hd2_5.text: If you rely on legitimate interest, summarise the balancing test.
hd2_5.helpText: Record the interest, the necessity and the balance against the individuals' rights; a full LIA can be attached. Source: GDPR Art. 6(1)(f), DPO Central LIA template.

hd3_1.text: What are the sources of the data (websites, apps, pages, partners)?
hd3_1.helpText: Source: 11 CCR 7152(a)(1) to (3); GDPR Art. 35(7)(a) (checked 16 September 2026).

options: Pixel or tag on web pages
Data received from partners or data brokers

hd3_3.text: Which categories of data are processed, field by field?
hd3_3.helpText: List each field and event: event names, page URLs and paths, search terms, product categories, device identifiers, IP address, location. Mark any field that can reveal a health condition.

hd3_4.text: How long is each category kept, by you and by each recipient?

hd3_5.text: Which consumers are affected, and how many?
hd3_5.helpText: Include minors and other vulnerable groups where relevant.

hd3_6.text: Who receives the data, and in what role?
hd3_6.helpText: For each recipient give the role: service provider, contractor or third party (CCPA); processor or controller (GDPR). Source: DPO Central jurisdiction catalogue, CCPA/CPRA and GDPR entry.

hd3_7.text: Which disclosures to third parties take place, and is any of them a sale or sharing?

hd4_1.text: What are the benefits to the business?

hd4_2.text: What are the benefits to consumers?

hd4_3.text: What are the benefits to the public, if any?

hd5_1.text: Which negative impacts could the processing cause?
options: Loss of consumer control over their data

hd5_2.text: For each impact selected, describe how it could occur, its likelihood and its severity.

hd6_1.text: Factor 1, source: where does the data come from?
hd6_1.helpText: Options are in rising order of risk (0 to 3). Method of this template, not a legal test: the five factors follow the NAI Factor Analysis (2026), and the scoring and the bands are the template's own.
options: General-audience context with no link to health
Healthcare provider, pharmacy or health app

hd6_2.text: Factor 2, content: what does the data say?
options: An indirect indicator, such as a product category
A health interest or an inferred condition
A specific condition or treatment, or reproductive or sexual health

hd6_3.text: Factor 3, use: how is the data used?
options: Audience segment based on a health interest
Targeting or excluding individuals by health condition

hd6_4.text: Factor 4, expectations: would consumers expect this use?
options: Consumers probably do not expect it

hd6_5.text: Factor 5, harm: how serious would the harm be if the data were misused or disclosed?
options: Severe (for example discrimination or disclosure of a condition)

hd7_1.text: Which main mitigation route do you choose?
options: Suppress health-related data for consumers in opt-in states
Rely on partner due diligence and contract controls
Avoid high-risk campaigns (no targeting on health conditions)
De-identify the data before any disclosure

hd7_2.helpText: Colorado, Connecticut and Texas recognise universal opt-out mechanisms. Source: DPO Central jurisdiction catalogue, CPA, CTDPA and TDPSA entry.
options: Remove URL paths, search terms and parameters from pixel and SDK events
Contract terms prohibiting re-identification and onward use
Partner due diligence before any disclosure

hd7_3.text: Describe the partner due diligence and the contract terms in place.

hd8_1.text: Washington or Nevada: do you obtain the consumer's consent before collecting consumer health data, and separate consent before sharing it?
hd8_1.helpText: Answer Yes or No; add the detail in the notes. Source: Washington RCW 19.373.030; Nevada NRS 603A.500 (checked 16 September 2026).

hd8_2.text: Washington or Nevada: is any consumer health data sold, and if so, do you hold a valid signed authorisation from each consumer?
hd8_2.helpText: Answer Yes only if there is no sale, or every sale is covered by a signed authorisation naming the data, the seller and each purchaser. Source: Washington RCW 19.373.070; Nevada NRS 603A.535 (checked 16 September 2026).

hd8_3.text: Washington or Nevada: do you use a geofence around places where health care is provided to identify, track or send messages to consumers?
hd8_3.helpText: This geofencing is prohibited: within 2,000 feet of in-person health care in Washington, within 1,750 feet of a medical facility in Nevada. A Yes is reported as a breach to resolve. Source: RCW 19.373.080; NRS 603A.540 (checked 16 September 2026).

hd8_4.text: Maryland: does any disclosure amount to a sale of sensitive data, including health data?
hd8_4.helpText: Maryland prohibits the sale of sensitive data; it is not only an opt-out, and consent does not make such a sale lawful. Sensitive data may be processed only where strictly necessary for a product or service the consumer requested. Source: Md. Com. Law 14-4607(a)(1),(2) (2024 ch. 454; checked 16 September 2026).

hd8_5.text: California: do you offer and honour the right to limit the use and disclosure of sensitive personal information?
hd8_5.helpText: Source: DPO Central jurisdiction catalogue, CCPA/CPRA entry.

hd8_6.text: California: on what date was this risk assessment documented, and when is the abridged filing due?
hd8_6.helpText: Timetable: assess before the processing starts; processing begun before 2026 must be assessed by 31 December 2027; summary information and an executive attestation are submitted to CalPrivacy by 1 April 2028; the full report is produced within 30 days of a request. Use the format YYYY-MM-DD. Source: 11 CCR 7155(a),(b) and 7157(a),(e) (checked 16 September 2026).

hd8_7.text: California: which executive will sign the attestation that accompanies the filing (name and title)?
hd8_7.helpText: The attestation is made under penalty of perjury by a member of executive management who is directly responsible for risk-assessment compliance. Source: 11 CCR 7157(b)(5),(c) (checked 16 September 2026).

hd8_8.text: US states: do you obtain opt-in consent before processing sensitive data, including health data?
hd8_8.helpText: Source: DPO Central jurisdiction catalogue, CTDPA, CPA, VCDPA, TDPSA and OCPA entry. For other states, check each law [to verify]. In Maryland, consent does not permit a sale.

hd8_9.text: US states: can consumers opt out of targeted advertising and the sale of their data?
hd8_9.helpText: Source: DPO Central jurisdiction catalogue, CTDPA, CPA, VCDPA, TDPSA and OCPA (right to opt out) entry. The exact scope of the opt-out in each state [to verify].

hd8_10.text: EU/EEA or UK: did you seek the advice of the data protection officer on this DPIA?
hd8_10.helpText: Source: DPO Central DPIA template (consultation section).

hd9_1.text: What is the residual risk after the safeguards?
hd9_1.helpText: Source: DPO Central DPIA template (GDPR Art. 35 and Art. 36 questions).

options: Proceed only after prior consultation with the supervisory authority

hd9_3.text: EU/EEA or UK: is prior consultation with the supervisory authority required (Art. 36)?
hd9_3.helpText: Required where the DPIA shows a high risk that the measures do not reduce. The report flags it when the residual risk is High or Very high. Source: DPO Central DPIA template (GDPR Art. 35 and Art. 36 questions).

hd10_1.text: Executive who approves and signs (name and title)
hd10_1.helpText: Record also who contributed to the assessment. Source: 11 CCR 7152(a)(7) to (9) (checked 16 September 2026).

hd10_3.helpText: Review at least when the processing, the partners or the law change.

q1_1.text: What categories of personal data will be processed?
q1_1.helpText: List all data categories (e.g. identifiers, financial, behavioral, special category). Be specific about each category.

q1_2.text: What is the purpose of the processing?
q1_2.helpText: Describe the primary and any secondary purposes. Reference specific business objectives.

q1_3.text: What is the legal basis for processing?

q1_5.text: Estimated number of data subjects affected

q1_6.text: Describe the data flows and recipients
q1_6.helpText: Map how data moves through your systems, from collection to storage, processing, sharing, and deletion. Identify all recipients and processors.

q2_1.text: What is the sensitivity level of the data?
options: Mix of non-sensitive and sensitive indicators
Includes special category data (Art. 9) or criminal offense data (Art. 10)

q2_2.helpText: State retention periods for each data category and justify why that duration is necessary.

q2_3.helpText: Identify all countries where data is processed or stored, and the transfer mechanisms used (e.g. adequacy decision, SCCs, BCRs).

q2_4.text: Would data subjects reasonably expect this processing?
options: Fully expected: directly related to the service they signed up for
Probably expected: a reasonable extension of the service
Possibly unexpected: not directly related to the primary service
Unexpected: data subjects would likely be surprised

q3_1.text: Is the processing necessary to achieve the stated purpose?
options: Essential: cannot achieve the purpose without it
Highly beneficial: significantly more effective than alternatives
Somewhat beneficial: marginal improvement over alternatives
Not clearly necessary: alternatives could achieve the same result

q3_2.text: What alternatives were considered and why were they rejected?
q3_2.helpText: Describe less intrusive alternatives you evaluated and explain why the chosen approach is necessary.

q3_3.text: What data minimization measures are in place?
q3_3.helpText: Describe measures to ensure only necessary data is collected and processed (e.g. pseudonymization, aggregation, field-level restrictions).

q4_1.text: Who was consulted during this assessment?

q4_2.text: Summary of consultation outcomes and actions taken
q4_2.helpText: Summarize feedback received, objections raised, and any changes made to the processing as a result.

q5_1.text: Does the processing involve automated decision-making or profiling?

q5_2.text: Does the processing involve special category data or criminal offense data?

q5_3.text: Does the processing involve systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area?

q5_4.text: Is the processing carried out on a large scale?

q5_5.text: Does the processing involve innovative use of technology (e.g. AI, biometrics, IoT)?

q5_6.text: Describe the identified risks to data subjects, including likelihood and severity for each
q5_6.helpText: For each risk: describe the source and the rights affected, and grade its likelihood and its severity on the same four levels (Negligible / Limited / Significant / Maximum). Then add each risk to the risk register, where it is graded before and after the measures.

q6_1.text: Technical measures in place or planned

q6_2.text: Organizational measures in place or planned

q6_3.text: Safeguards for individual rights (transparency, consent mechanisms, portability, opt-out)
q6_3.helpText: Describe how data subject rights are facilitated (e.g. privacy notices, consent preference centers, data portability tools, opt-out mechanisms).

q7_1.text: Overall residual risk level after mitigations

q7_2.text: Is prior consultation with the supervisory authority required? (Art. 36)
options: No: residual risk has been sufficiently mitigated
Yes: high residual risk that cannot be sufficiently mitigated

q7_3.helpText: Record the DPO's formal advice: whether the processing may proceed, any conditions, and the recommended review date.

system-pia-template-v2.name: Privacy Impact Assessment
system-pia-template-v2.description: A broad privacy review of a processing activity: the data, the purposes, the lawful basis, retention, recipients, the rights of individuals and security, with structured answers.

piav2_s1.title: The processing
piav2_s1.description: Describe what is processed, why and about whom.

piav2_s2.title: Lawful basis and retention
piav2_s2.description: Record the lawful basis and how long the data is kept.

piav2_s3.title: Recipients and transfers
piav2_s3.description: Record who receives the data and any transfer abroad.

piav2_s4.title: Rights and transparency
piav2_s4.description: Record how individuals are informed and how their rights are met.

piav2_s5.title: Security and outcome
piav2_s5.description: Record the security measures and the overall privacy risk.

piav2_1_1.text: What is the purpose of the processing?
piav2_1_1.helpText: State the specific, explicit purpose, which every later question is measured against. Example: "Managing customer orders and after-sales support." Source: GDPR Art. 5(1)(b).

piav2_1_2.text: What categories of personal data are processed?
piav2_1_2.helpText: List every category, because the categories drive the risk and the obligations. Example: "Contact details, identifiers, financial data." Source: GDPR Art. 30(1)(c).

piav2_1_3.text: Does the processing involve special category or criminal-offense data?
piav2_1_3.helpText: Special category data (Art. 9) and criminal-offense data (Art. 10) need a specific condition beyond the lawful basis. Example: "No." Source: GDPR Arts. 9 and 10.

piav2_1_4.text: Which Article 9(2) or Article 10 condition applies?
piav2_1_4.helpText: Name the specific condition that permits the special category or criminal-offense data. Example: "Explicit consent (Art. 9(2)(a))." Source: GDPR Arts. 9(2) and 10.

piav2_1_5.helpText: Name the groups whose data is processed. Children and vulnerable people call for extra care. Example: "Customers and website users." Source: GDPR Art. 30(1)(c); Recital 38.

piav2_2_1.text: What is the lawful basis for the processing?
piav2_2_1.helpText: Every processing needs one of the six lawful bases, chosen before processing begins. Legitimate interest also needs a balancing test (the LIA template). Example: "Contract." Source: GDPR Art. 6(1).

piav2_2_2.text: How long is the data kept, and from when?
piav2_2_2.helpText: State a retention period and its starting point, not "as long as necessary". Example: "6 years from the end of the contract, for tax law." Source: GDPR Art. 5(1)(e).

piav2_2_3.text: Is the retention period justified and enforced?
piav2_2_3.helpText: The period must be justified by the purpose or a legal duty, and the data actually deleted or anonymized at the end. Example: "Yes: annual deletion job removes expired records." Source: GDPR Art. 5(1)(e).

piav2_3_1.helpText: Name every category of recipient, because each adds obligations and risk. Example: "Internal teams and a hosting processor." Source: GDPR Art. 30(1)(d).

piav2_3_2.text: Is every processor bound by a written data processing agreement (Art. 28)?
piav2_3_2.helpText: A processor may only act under a contract with the terms Article 28 requires. Example: "Yes: a signed DPA is in place with each processor." Source: GDPR Art. 28(3).

piav2_3_3.text: Is any data transferred outside the EU or EEA?
piav2_3_3.helpText: A transfer to a third country needs a transfer tool and, outside adequacy, a Transfer Impact Assessment (the TIA template). Example: "Yes: our hosting provider is in the United States." Source: GDPR Arts. 44 to 49.

piav2_3_4.text: Which transfer tool covers it, and is a TIA in place?
piav2_3_4.helpText: Name the transfer tool and whether a Transfer Impact Assessment has been done. Example: "Standard Contractual Clauses; TIA completed 2026-05." Source: GDPR Arts. 46 and 44.

piav2_4_1.text: Have individuals been given the privacy information required by Articles 13-14?
piav2_4_1.helpText: People must be told who processes their data, why, on what basis, for how long and what rights they have. Example: "Yes: a layered privacy notice at the point of collection." Source: GDPR Arts. 13 and 14.

piav2_4_2.text: Which data subject rights are supported?
piav2_4_2.helpText: You must be able to honor the rights that apply to your basis and processing. Example: "Access, rectification, erasure and objection." Source: GDPR Arts. 15 to 22.

piav2_4_3.text: Is there solely automated decision-making with legal or similarly significant effects?
piav2_4_3.helpText: Decisions made solely by automated means with a legal or similarly significant effect are restricted and need specific safeguards. Example: "No: a person reviews every decision." Source: GDPR Art. 22.

piav2_4_4.text: What safeguards apply to the automated decision-making?
piav2_4_4.helpText: Describe the lawful ground and the safeguards: the right to human intervention, to express a view and to contest the decision. Example: "Explicit consent; the person can request a human review." Source: GDPR Art. 22(3).

piav2_5_1.text: Which security measures protect the data (Art. 32)?
piav2_5_1.helpText: Measures must be appropriate to the risk, covering confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience. Example: "Encryption, access controls, backups and logging." Source: GDPR Art. 32.

piav2_5_2.text: What is the overall privacy risk after these measures?
piav2_5_2.helpText: Give the residual risk once the measures are in place. A high residual risk points to a full DPIA and possibly prior consultation. Example: "Low." Source: GDPR Arts. 35 and 36.

piav2_5_3.text: What residual actions or recommendations remain?
piav2_5_3.helpText: Note any follow-up needed to reduce the risk further or to keep the assessment current. Example: "Schedule a DPIA if profiling is added." Source: GDPR Art. 35(1).

applicability.cardDescription: A few plain questions about how you use personal data. With the jurisdictions you operate in, they show which laws and duties apply. Everything stays editable.
applicability.intro: Answer what you can. "Not sure yet" is fine: it shows as worth checking, never as settled.

actAsController.label: Do you decide why and how personal data is used?
actAsController.hint: If so, you are a controller for that data and carry the main duties.

actAsProcessor.label: Do you process personal data for other organizations on their instructions?
actAsProcessor.hint: If so, you are a processor for that data, bound by a written contract.

largeVolume.label: Are you a large business by revenue or by the number of people whose data you handle?
largeVolume.hint: For example the CCPA's thresholds: high annual revenue, or the data of 100,000+ consumers.

sensitiveData.label: Do you process special category data, such as health, race, religion or biometric data?
sensitiveData.hint: This data carries extra duties under the GDPR (Art. 9).

children.label: Do you process children's personal data?
children.hint: Children's data raises the bar for consent, notices and impact assessments.

largeScaleMonitoring.label: Do you monitor people regularly and systematically on a large scale?
largeScaleMonitoring.hint: For example tracking online behavior, profiling, or wide video surveillance.

publicAuthority.label: Are you a public authority or body?
publicAuthority.hint: Public authorities must appoint a data protection officer.

ccpaRequests.clockNote: The 45-day period starts on the day the request is received, even while identity is being verified. Confirm receipt within 10 business days and say how the request will be handled and when to expect an answer.

know.label: Right to know
know.desc: What personal information the business collected, used, sold or shared about the consumer, including the specific pieces.

delete.label: Right to delete
delete.desc: Delete the personal information the business holds about the consumer.

correct.label: Right to correct
correct.desc: Correct inaccurate personal information the business maintains about the consumer.

ccpaRequests.clock45: 45 calendar days from receipt; extendable once by 45 more days when reasonably necessary, if the consumer is told within the first 45 days.

optOut.label: Opt out of sale or sharing
optOut.desc: Stop selling or sharing the consumer's personal information. The business may not require a verifiable consumer request.

limit.label: Limit use of sensitive personal information
limit.desc: Limit the use and disclosure of the consumer's sensitive personal information. The business may not require a verifiable consumer request.

ccpaRequests.clock15: As soon as feasibly possible and no later than 15 business days from receipt; no extension.
